readerTitle: Your moisturizer sells out at home. Now a buyer abroad wants it.
caseNote: 가상 사례 (스킨케어 브랜드, 라멘 가게) · 적용 레슨으로 STR-10-03(현지화 vs 표준화), STR-10-04(시장 진입 방식)를 함께 사용
insight: 해외 진출은 '무엇을 바꿀까'와 '얼마나 깊이 들어갈까'라는 두 결정이다. 정체성은 지키고 고객이 매일 느끼는 부분만 맞추며, 배우는 동안에는 되돌릴 수 있는 방식으로 들어간다.
misconception: 잘 팔리는 제품이면 그대로 가져가도 되고, 진출할 때는 처음부터 크게 계약해야 빨리 자리 잡는다.

sources.text: 이 유닛의 개념 레슨 STR-10-03(현지화 vs 표준화), STR-10-04(시장 진입 방식)을 적용
모든 사례와 인물은 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 화장품의 성분·표시·효능 문구 규정이 나라마다 다르다는 점은 일반적인 사실로만 적었습니다. 특정 국가의 규정이나 허가 절차는 다루지 않았습니다. 게시 전 표현이 법률 조언처럼 읽히지 않는지 확인하세요.
진입 방식 사다리(직접 수출 → 유통 파트너 → 라이선스·프랜차이즈 → 자회사·직영)는 STR-10-04의 용어와 순서가 일치하는지 확인하세요.
수치는 쓰지 않았습니다. 모든 장면은 가상 사례이며 실제 브랜드를 연상시키는 이름을 쓰지 않았습니다.

cards.title: Your moisturizer sells out at home. Now a buyer abroad wants it.
body: Mina runs a small skincare brand in a humid coastal city. Her light gel moisturizer is the bestseller, and customers love the clean, plain packaging.
One morning, an email arrives from a beauty retailer in a cold, dry country far away. They want to stock her line. Mina has two big decisions to make, and the first one is about what goes in the box.

image.label: A skincare jar on a desk next to an open email from abroad
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 책상 위에 심플한 흰색 젤 크림 용기 하나, 옆 노트북 화면에 해외에서 온 이메일(내용은 흐릿하게). 창밖 절반은 습한 바닷가, 절반은 눈 내리는 도시로 나뉜 연출. 실제 브랜드 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: What should change for the new market?
body: The retailer says customers there have dry skin in winter, read a different language, and usually buy larger jars.
Mina has limited time and money. What does she change?

options.text: Nothing. The product works, so ship it exactly as it is
options.feedback: Full **standardization** keeps costs low and the brand consistent. But a light gel may feel thin in a dry winter, and a label customers can't read won't sell.

options.text: Rebuild it for them: new formula, new name, new look
options.feedback: Heavy **localization** fits the market, but it costs a lot and throws away what made the brand worth stocking in the first place.

options.text: Keep the brand and hero ingredient. Adapt texture, label and jar size
options.feedback: This is **localize or standardize** used well: keep what makes the brand yours, and change only what customers there feel every day.

cards.title: Split the product into what's yours and what must fit.
body: Mina goes line by line. Each part gets one of two labels: keep it the same everywhere, or adapt it to the market.

breakdown.label: Brand name and look
breakdown.detail: The clean packaging is why the retailer called

breakdown.label: Texture
breakdown.detail: A richer winter version of the same gel

breakdown.label: Label and claims
breakdown.detail: Local language, and wording that fits local rules

breakdown.label: Jar size
breakdown.detail: Match how people there usually buy

cards.title: How should Mina get into the market?
body: The retailer offers a deal: exclusive rights to sell her line in the whole country for five years, starting with a large first order.
Mina has never sold there before. What should she do?

options.text: Decline and sell directly to customers there through her own website
options.feedback: Direct export keeps full control and the customer data. But shipping is slow and costly, and almost no one there knows her name yet.

options.text: Sign the five-year exclusive deal to grow fast
options.feedback: Big commitment buys speed, but if sales disappoint or the partner underperforms, she's locked out of the country for years.

options.text: Offer a one-year trial in a few stores, non-exclusive, with clear goals to extend
options.feedback: This uses **ways to enter a market**: a light entry that borrows the partner's reach while she learns, and stays easy to undo.

cards.title: Go deeper only as fast as you learn.
body: Entry options run from light to heavy: selling directly from home, working with a local partner, licensing your brand, or opening your own operation. Each step up brings more control and more cost, and it's harder to reverse.
Mina's first decision feeds her second. She doesn't yet know if the winter texture works. A **light, reversible entry** lets her find out before she bets on it.

image.label: A ladder of entry options from light to heavy commitment
image.brief: 인포그래픽. 왼쪽에서 오른쪽으로 올라가는 계단 4칸: "Sell direct", "Local partner", "License", "Own operation". 계단 위로 "More control" 화살표, 아래로 "More cost, harder to undo" 화살표. 두 번째 칸에 작은 스킨케어 용기가 서 있음.

cards.title: Every change and every partner has a hidden cost.
body: Each adapted version is a separate product to make, test, stock and track. A small brand with three markets and three textures can quickly drown in inventory.

A partner also brings a trade-off. They know the shelf, the buyers and the customers. That's why the deal is attractive. But they often own the customer relationship, too. Ask early what sales and customer information you'll get back.
cards.softwareNote: The same two decisions show up for software. Translating the interface and taking local payment methods are cheap adaptations. Rebuilding features per country is expensive. Many software companies enter through a local reseller before hiring their own team.

cards.title: Now it's a ramen shop.
body: Your ramen shop is famous at home for a slow-cooked broth. A local operator abroad wants to open a franchise. Locals there usually prefer milder food and smaller lunch portions.
What do you lock in across both countries?

options.text: Lock the broth recipe and cooking process. Let spice level, portions and side dishes adapt
options.feedback: **Localize or standardize** again: the broth is the identity, so it stays fixed. The rest is how customers there like to eat.

options.text: Let the operator change anything that sells better
options.feedback: Sales may come fast, but a franchise that drifts from the broth stops being your brand, and it can hurt your name at home.

options.text: Copy everything exactly, down to portions and hours
options.feedback: Consistency is safe for the brand, but a bowl too big and too spicy for local lunch habits leaves seats empty.

cards.callout: A franchise is itself an entry choice: fast reach through a partner, in exchange for less day-to-day control.

cards.title: Keep what's yours, adapt what they feel, and enter in a way you can undo.
body: **Concepts used:** *Localize or standardize* to sort the product, and *ways to enter a market* to choose a light, reversible first step.
**Try it today:** list five parts of your product or service. Mark each one "keep everywhere" or "adapt locally." Then circle the one that would hurt most to get wrong.
